passage:
Daycare note, Thursday, from Ayesha (room teacher)

To Farhan's mother: when I said "garden time", Farhan flapped his hands, bounced on his toes and squealed. Two other children started bouncing too! He ran round the slide again and again. When I called everyone in, he flopped on the grass and sobbed. I sat beside him and we waved goodbye to the slide together. After a drink of water he settled and joined story time. 🙂

qa.q: What did Farhan do when Ayesha said "garden time"?
qa.a: He flapped his hands, bounced on his toes and squealed.

qa.q: What was Farhan most likely feeling when he flopped on the grass and sobbed?
qa.a: Most likely disappointed that the fun was ending after such a big build-up of excitement. He may also have been hot or thirsty, since he settled after a drink of water.

qa.q: What small step could help Farhan when garden time ends another day?
qa.a: A warning a few minutes before, such as "two more turns, then goodbye slide", could make the ending feel less sudden.

qa.q: How are the other children affected by Farhan's excitement?
qa.a: His excitement spreads to them: two of them start bouncing too, so his joy lifts the whole group.

grounding: It shows a toddler's bodily, catching excitement before an outing and the tears that come when it ends.

passage:
Note from Pranav at the creche, for Sunaina's parents

Today a balloon burst near the window. Sunaina's eyes went wide, she gasped and went stiff all over. Her lip started to wobble and she looked straight at me. I smiled, kept my voice slow and said, "Pop! Big noise." Then I clapped once, softly. She stared at me, then giggled and clapped too. All afternoon she kept whispering "pop!" to her doll. 😊

qa.q: What burst near the window?
qa.a: A balloon burst near the window.

qa.q: What does Sunaina's wobbling lip and her look at Pranav suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She was most likely startled and a little frightened by the sudden bang, and looked at Pranav to check whether she was safe. Her giggle a moment later shows the surprise could also tip into amusement.

qa.q: Which choice worked here, and why?
qa.a: Pranav stayed calm, smiled and named the noise in a slow voice, so Sunaina read that she was safe and her surprise turned into laughter.

qa.q: What would change if Pranav had jumped and shouted too?
qa.a: Sunaina would probably have picked up Pranav's alarm, and her surprise might have turned into crying and fear instead of a game.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler's wide-eyed, gasping surprise at a sudden sound turning to laughter because the caregiver stays calm.

passage:
Monday: Chinmay skipped his afternoon nap. By five he was rubbing his eyes, whining and hanging off his father's leg. At the vegetable stall he threw himself on the floor and kicked. "Stop being naughty," Saurabh snapped.

Wednesday: the same eye-rubbing, the same clinging. Saurabh glanced at the clock. No nap again. He drew the curtains and lay down beside his son. Chinmay was asleep within minutes.

Saturday: nap first, market after. Chinmay pointed at every tomato and laughed.

qa.q: Where did Chinmay throw himself on the floor?
qa.a: At the vegetable stall.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling when he rubbed his eyes and clung to his father's leg?
qa.a: Most likely overtired and cranky, since he had skipped his nap and fell asleep quickly once the room was dark. Another possible reading is that he was bored or hungry at the stall.

qa.q: What went wrong on Monday, and what fixed it later?
qa.a: Saurabh treated the meltdown as naughtiness, but the real problem was a missed nap. Putting sleep first on Saturday meant a happy trip to the market.

qa.q: How does Saurabh's view of the meltdowns change between Monday and Wednesday?
qa.a: On Monday he sees naughtiness and snaps, but by Wednesday he connects the clinging to the missed nap and responds with rest instead of scolding.

grounding: It shows a toddler's eye-rubbing, whining and meltdown when overtired being mistaken for naughtiness until rest fixes it.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage:
From Usha to Tanvir's mother, Tuesday

Tanvir cried hard at half past eleven. First I checked him all over: no bump, no scratch, nappy dry. It was near lunch, so I offered rice. He pushed the bowl away and cried louder. Then I saw his tower of cups had fallen. I sat on the mat and we built it again together. He sniffed, then laughed when it toppled. I think the tower was the trouble today, not hunger.

qa.q: What did Usha offer Tanvir because it was near lunch?
qa.a: She offered him rice.

qa.q: What was Tanvir most likely feeling when he cried?
qa.a: Most likely frustrated that his tower of cups had fallen, since he calmed once they rebuilt it. Being tired just before lunch could also have made him less patient.

qa.q: How did Usha work out what the tears meant?
qa.a: Usha checked his body first, then tried food, then looked around the room, and only then decided what the tears were about.

qa.q: If you were Tanvir's mother, what would you learn from the note?
qa.a: That Tanvir was not hurt or hungry, and that a fallen tower can upset him a lot, so she would know what to watch for at home.

grounding: It illustrates a caregiver checking the body and setting before deciding that a toddler's tears came from frustration.

passage:
Tuesday: Rukmini screamed and threw her shoe across the hall. Pallavi picked it up and made it talk in a squeaky voice. Two minutes later Rukmini was giggling and trying to feed the shoe a biscuit.

Thursday: another tantrum over the bath, gone as soon as a rubber duck appeared.

Saturday: the crying started after breakfast and did not stop. Rukmini kept tugging at one ear and pushed the duck away. Pallavi stopped trying tricks and phoned the clinic for a visit.

qa.q: What did Pallavi make the shoe do on Tuesday?
qa.a: Pallavi made it talk in a squeaky voice.

qa.q: What was Rukmini most likely feeling on Saturday?
qa.a: She was most likely hurting or unwell, since she kept tugging at one ear and nothing cheered her. She might also have been very tired, but the long crying made Pallavi take it seriously.

qa.q: Which choice on Saturday was wise, and why?
qa.a: Pallavi stopped using distractions and phoned the clinic, because crying that lasts and does not respond to comfort can mean a real need.

qa.q: What is it like for Pallavi when the usual tricks stop working?
qa.a: It is probably worrying for Pallavi, because the quick fixes that worked all week now fail, and that change is a sign that something is different.

grounding: It shows a toddler's short outbursts that pass with distraction, contrasted with lasting crying that points to a real need.

passage:
Week one: the pressure cooker whistled and Suraj burst into a belly laugh, head thrown back. Salma laughed too.

Week three: Salma was on a long phone call. Suraj squeezed his eyes shut and wailed, but no tears came. Between wails he peeked to see if she was watching.

Salma ended the call and sat on the floor. "You want me, don't you?" He climbed into her lap, quiet at once.

Next morning she played with him before her calls, and he fetched his book.

qa.q: What made Suraj laugh in week one?
qa.a: The pressure cooker whistled.

qa.q: Why did Suraj peek between his wails?
qa.a: He was most likely feeling lonely and left out while Salma talked, and was checking whether his crying got her attention. Another reading is that he was simply bored during the long call.

qa.q: How could a parent respond to a fake cry like Suraj's?
qa.a: Like Salma, a parent can look at the need underneath, which here was attention, and meet it calmly, even planning time together before calls.

qa.q: How does Salma see Suraj's tearless wail?
qa.a: She sees it as a sign that he wants her, not as naughtiness, so she answers with closeness rather than scolding.

grounding: It shows a toddler moving from a spontaneous laugh to a deliberate fake cry, and a parent responding to the need underneath.

passage:
Sunday: Nitin tripped on the steps and wailed. Pooja scooped him up. Halfway through a sob he smiled at her, tears still running. "See, he's fine," said his aunt, and set him down. He crumpled and cried again.

The next Friday he fell in the park. Pooja held him close. He smiled through the tears again, but this time she kept holding him until the hiccupping sobs stopped.

Later that day he went down the park steps holding the rail, glancing back at her.

qa.q: Who set Nitin down on Sunday?
qa.a: His aunt set him down.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when he smiled through his tears?
qa.a: Most likely a mix of relief at being held and hurt from the fall; the smile showed comfort was working, not that the pain was gone. He may also have been a little embarrassed after the trip.

qa.q: What did Pooja do differently in the park, and why did it help?
qa.a: She kept holding him until the sobs stopped, following the crying rather than the smile, so he finished calming down properly.

qa.q: Why might the aunt read the smile differently from Pooja?
qa.a: The aunt saw the smile and assumed he was fine, while Pooja noticed the tears were still running and treated him as still upset.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler smiling while still crying after a fall, and comfort that follows the crying, not the smile.

passage:
The power went out just as Hrithik opened the feelings book, so he held a torch over the page for his little sister.

"This girl's face?" he asked.

Afreen squinted at the wide eyes and open mouth. "Surprised! Like a birthday."

Hrithik turned back one page in the jumpy light. A huge dog was bounding towards the girl.

"What happened just before?"

Afreen looked again, frowning. "The dog came... She's scared. Not birthday surprised."

The torch flickered, and they both laughed.

qa.q: What was bounding towards the girl on the page before?
qa.a: A huge dog.

qa.q: How can you tell Afreen felt unsure about the face at first?
qa.a: She guessed "surprised" quickly, then frowned and changed her answer once she saw the dog, so she was probably confused between surprise and fear. The dim torchlight may also have made the face hard to see.

qa.q: What small step helped Afreen read the face correctly?
qa.a: Asking what happened just before the picture gave her the clue she needed, without Hrithik telling her the answer.

qa.q: Why might Hrithik ask about the page before instead of giving the answer?
qa.a: He probably wanted Afreen to work it out herself, so she could use the same trick of looking at what came before on other faces.

grounding: It shows a preschooler confusing fear with surprise and a simple question about what happened just before helping her read the face.

passage:
"Rrraaar! I'm the monster!" Sonali curled her fingers, bared her teeth and scrunched her nose.

"Arre, why so angry?" Dadi called from the sofa.

"She's not angry, Dadi," said Joseph from next door. "Look, she's giggling."

"Rrraa... hee hee!"

"Monster, you're laughing!"

"Monsters can laugh!" Sonali stomped with her arms wide, her snarl cracking into a grin. "Now you run!"

Joseph shrieked and dived behind the sofa.

Dadi chuckled. "Ah. A happy monster."

"The scariest kind," Joseph whispered.

qa.q: Where did Joseph dive to hide?
qa.a: He dived behind the sofa.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling while she snarled like a monster?
qa.a: She was most likely enjoying herself and feeling playful; her giggles and grin kept breaking through the scowl. Dadi's first reading, that she was angry, shows the face alone can look like real anger.

qa.q: How could an adult tell play anger from real anger in a scene like this?
qa.a: By looking beyond the face at the giggling, the loose stomping body and the game going on, as Joseph pointed out.

qa.q: How does Joseph see Sonali's monster face?
qa.a: He knows it is part of the game and even enjoys being scared, shrieking and hiding while pointing out her giggles to Dadi.

grounding: It illustrates a child's posed monster scowl in pretend play and how giggling and a playful body show it is not real anger.

passage:
Ritu Didi searched the whole flat in Pune before she found her phone inside the rice tin. She walked into the living room holding it up, grains still stuck to the cover.

"Hafsa. Anything to tell me?"

Hafsa pressed her lips tightly together and stared hard at the ceiling fan. Her cheeks puffed out. Her eyes, though, were crinkling at the corners, and a tiny snort escaped.

"I don't know," she squeaked.

Ritu Didi bit the inside of her cheek. "Rice phone. Very clever. Not again, okay?"

qa.q: Where did Ritu Didi find her phone?
qa.a: Inside the rice tin.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when she pressed her lips together and stared at the fan?
qa.a: Most likely amused and a little proud of her trick, while knowing she was supposed to look sorry. She may also have felt nervous about being in trouble.

qa.q: How did Ritu Didi handle the moment well?
qa.a: She stayed light but still set a limit with "Not again, okay?", so Hafsa learnt the rule without being shamed.

qa.q: How does Ritu Didi see Hafsa's squashed smile?
qa.a: She reads the crinkled eyes and snort as a giveaway, and finds it so funny that she has to bite her own cheek.

grounding: It shows a child pressing her lips together to hold back a smile after mischief, with the amusement leaking through her eyes.
